title: On the Road
description: Published by Viking on 5 September 1957: Sal Paradise's account of his journeys across America in 1947-50 with Dean Moriarty, a young ex-convict and car thief, in a book that made the road, the car and the jazz club the images of postwar American freedom.
plot_or_argument: Sal Paradise, a young writer living with his aunt in Paterson, New Jersey, has just finished a book and is recovering from a divorce when he meets Dean Moriarty, a wild, handsome, fast-talking young man from Denver who has spent time in reformatories and is newly married to a girl called Marylou. Part One follows Sal's first journey west in July 1947 - the buses and the hitch-hiking, the nights in Denver with Dean and their friend Carlo Marx, the ghost town of Central City, the job as a night watchman near San Francisco, the affair with Terry, a Mexican girl, and the cotton fields of California - and his return to New York. Part Two is the winter of 1948-49, when Dean arrives at Christmas with Marylou and the Dodge, and Sal, Dean and Marylou drive to New Orleans and on to San Francisco, where Dean abandons Sal for his wife Camille. Part Three is the spring of 1949: Sal in Denver, a trip to Mexico City, and Dean's arrival to take him to New York, where Sal meets the woman he calls 'the girl' and Dean leaves. Part Four is 1950, the great journey to Mexico with Dean, Sal and the poet Remi Boncoeur, and Part Five is the return to New York and Dean's last, brief appearance before he goes back west. The book's famous scenes - the drive to the Mexican border, the jazz clubs of San Francisco and New York, the 'mad ones' speech - are held together by Dean's energy and by Sal's growing awareness that the freedom he admires is also a form of irresponsibility.
narrative_structure: Five parts of very unequal length, each corresponding to a journey or a period in Sal's life; the narrative is episodic and picaresque, held together by the recurrence of Dean and by the first-person voice; the prose is spontaneous, paratactic and run on with dashes and colons, and the book's chronology is deliberately approximate.
meter_and_prosody: Kerouac's 'spontaneous bop prosody': long breathless sentences, strings of present participles, improvised lists of names and places, jazz-derived rhythms and repetitions; slang, profanity and Catholic devotional language side by side; a first-person narrator who is both inside and observing the action.
historical_context: Written in April 1951 on a continuous roll of taped-together paper in a three-week burst, then revised for years and heavily edited by Viking's editors before publication on 5 September 1957; the book's characters are portraits of Kerouac, Neal Cassady, Allen Ginsberg, William Burroughs and others, and its publication made Kerouac the spokesman of the Beat Generation and was received as a scandal and a manifesto at once.
literary_significance: The central novel of the Beat Generation and one of the defining American books of the 1950s; it named a youth culture, gave American prose a new speed and sound, has been continuously in print and widely taught since, and its manuscript roll is a canonical object of American literary history; it is the work through which the postwar counterculture and the road narrative are studied.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Viking Press (New York) on 5 September 1957; the original 1951 manuscript roll was published as On the Road: The Original Scroll (New York: Viking, 2007). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The novel's subject is the pursuit of 'it' - ecstasy, authenticity, the next party, the next saxophone solo - and its discovery that the pursuit destroys the people who follow it. Dean is both the novel's hero and its casualty: he leaves wives and children behind, steals cars and ends the book in rags, and Sal's love for him does not prevent the reader from seeing the damage. The road is the novel's image of American possibility and of American restlessness, and its landscape - the plains, the Denver mountains, the Mexican desert - is described with a lyricism that gives the book its lasting power. Behind the freedom is a melancholy, Catholic and Buddhist at once, that becomes explicit in Kerouac's later books.
summary: Five parts, three of them road trips with Dean, moving from Paterson, New Jersey, to Denver, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Mexico City, and filled with the people Sal and Dean meet on the way - hitch-hikers, waitresses, farm workers, musicians, junkies and friends.
critical_context: Criticism has read the novel as a picaresque, as a spiritual autobiography, as a document of postwar masculinity and of the Beats' marginalisation of women, and as a formal experiment in spontaneous prose. Its portraits of Cassady and Ginsberg and its treatment of race, class and sexuality have been much discussed, and the relation of the published text to the 1951 manuscript roll (published as On the Road: The Original Scroll in 2007) has become a subject of its own.
research_notes: The novel was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and quotations are limited to well-known phrases. The Norton selection is printed as an extract, and the record is the whole novel.

title: Harrison Bergeron
description: A story published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in October 1961 and collected in Welcome to the Monkey House (1968): in 2081 the United States has made everyone equal by law, and a fourteen-year-old boy who refuses his handicaps is shot dead on live television.
plot_or_argument: The story opens with the sentence that has become its signature: 'The year was 2081, and everybody was finally equal.' The equality is enforced by constitutional amendment and by the Handicapper General, Diana Moon Glampers, whose agents fit the strong with weights, the beautiful with masks and the intelligent with radios that broadcast noises into their ears every twenty seconds. George Bergeron, who is intelligent and strong, wears a forty-seven-pound bag of birdshot around his neck and a radio in his ear; his wife Hazel is of perfectly average intelligence and needs no handicap. They are watching a ballet on television - the ballerinas are masked and weighted - when a bulletin announces that their son Harrison, fourteen years old, seven feet tall and burdened with three hundred pounds of handicaps, has escaped from prison. Harrison storms the studio, tears off his handicaps and the ballerina's, declares himself emperor, chooses the ballerina as his empress and dances with her to the musicians' 'best' music. Diana Moon Glampers enters with a double-barrelled shotgun and kills them both; the television goes dark. George, who has left the room to get a beer, returns and asks Hazel why she has been crying; she says something sad happened on television but she cannot remember what it was.
narrative_structure: A single continuous scene of a few pages, with no chapters or breaks, in which the television broadcast, the parents' conversation and Harrison's irruption are intercut; the story's time is compressed into an evening and its exposition is delivered through the broadcast and the narrator's flat commentary.
meter_and_prosody: Short declarative sentences and very short paragraphs; a deadpan, faux-naive narrator who reports atrocity as ordinary fact; repeated phrases ('everybody was finally equal', 'that was the law') used as a refrain; dialogue in the flat idiom of television and bureaucracy; almost no metaphor, so that the few images (the birdshot bag, the shotgun) carry great weight.
historical_context: Published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction in October 1961 and collected in Welcome to the Monkey House (Delacorte, 1968); it belongs to Vonnegut's early period of magazine science fiction, written while he was working for General Electric and publishing in the slicks and the pulps, and it was adapted for television and film several times, most notably in the 1995 Showtime film.
literary_significance: One of the most widely anthologised American short stories of the century and a standard school text on dystopia, equality and the state; its opening sentence is one of the best known in American fiction, and the story is a frequent point of reference in political argument about merit and levelling, which has made it both unusually influential and unusually contested.
bibliographical_notes: First published in The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction, October 1961; collected in Welcome to the Monkey House (New York: Delacorte Press, 1968). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is a reductio ad absurdum of one reading of equality: a society that levels down every excellence to the lowest common denominator produces not justice but a numb, supervised mediocrity in which no one can think, feel or remember. Its satire is aimed at bureaucratic egalitarianism, and the story is regularly taught - and regularly contested - as an argument about equality and excellence; Vonnegut's own politics were egalitarian, and the story's target is more precisely the deadening of individuality by the state than equality as such. The ending, in which Hazel cannot remember her son's death, is the story's real horror: the handicaps have done their work on memory itself.
summary: A short story of some twelve hundred words set in 2081, in which George and Hazel Bergeron watch a television ballet, their son Harrison escapes from prison, seizes a studio and is killed by the Handicapper General, and his parents cannot remember what they have seen.
critical_context: The story has been read as a satire of enforced egalitarianism, as a Cold War parable about conformity and as a metafictional joke about the reader's own desire for a level playing field; critics have debated whether its target is equality itself (a reading Vonnegut resisted) or the bureaucratic administration of equality, and its portrait of Hazel and of the ballerinas has been central to feminist and disability readings of the story.
research_notes: Read through the text reproduced in anthologies and in the sources consulted; the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription.

title: Slaughterhouse-Five
description: Published by Delacorte on 31 March 1969, subtitled 'The Children's Crusade: A Duty-Dance with Death': the life of Billy Pilgrim, a prisoner of war in Dresden during the firebombing of 1945, who becomes 'unstuck in time' and is exhibited in a zoo on another planet, told in fragments by a narrator who is also a character.
plot_or_argument: The novel opens with a chapter in which 'I' - a narrator closely identified with Vonnegut - describes returning to Dresden in 1967 with his old war friend Bernard O'Hare, trying and failing for years to write a book about the firebombing, and beginning the book with the Children's Crusade and the famous first line 'All this happened, more or less.' The second chapter introduces Billy Pilgrim, an optometrist from Ilium, New York, who has come unstuck in time: he travels without warning between moments of his life, and the novel follows him through them. As a chaplain's assistant in 1944 he is captured in Luxembourg, survives the cattle cars, arrives in Dresden as a prisoner of war, and is working in a malt-syrup factory when the city is destroyed in February 1945; with the other prisoners he is put to work clearing the bodies. Later, abducted by the Tralfamadorians, he is kept in a zoo with the film star Montana Wildhack and learns their philosophy - that all moments exist simultaneously, that the dead are always alive in their own moments, and that the appropriate response to death is 'So it goes'. In the present of the novel's 1960s, Billy survives a plane crash, is nursed by his daughter, goes on television to tell the world about Tralfamadore, and is murdered in 1976 by Paul Lazzaro. The novel ends with the prisoners in Dresden and with the birdsong that follows the bombing, and with the narrator's acknowledgement that the book he has written is a failure and his son's war in Vietnam is not over.
narrative_structure: Ten chapters moving non-chronologically through Billy's life, with the narrator's own voice intruding in the first and last chapters and briefly in between; the Tralfamadorian episodes, the war, the optometrist's family life and the Dresden material are interleaved in short sections, so that the reader experiences time as Billy does. The book's fragments are held together by repeated phrases, by the refrain 'So it goes' and by the recurring image of the blue and ivory feet of the dead and dying.
meter_and_prosody: Short, flat sentences and very short paragraphs; deadpan irony and a naively precise notation of detail; refrain and repetition used as structure; lists, songs and doggerel poems embedded in the text; a tone that moves from slapstick to sorrow within a paragraph, and a narrator whose sentimentality is offered without embarrassment.
historical_context: Published by Delacorte Press on 31 March 1969 and dedicated to Mary O'Hare and Bernard V. O'Hare; Vonnegut had been a prisoner of war in Dresden and had worked for years on a book about it, visiting the city in 1967 with O'Hare. The novel appeared during the Vietnam War, was burned in a school board furnace in Drake, North Dakota, in 1973, and became one of the defining anti-war books of the American 1960s and 1970s; it was filmed by George Roy Hill in 1972.
literary_significance: Vonnegut's masterpiece and one of the central American novels of the postwar period; it is a standard text on the literature of war and of trauma, on postmodern narrative and on the 1960s, it has never been out of print, and its first chapter is often taught as an essay on the ethics of writing history.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Delacorte Press (New York) on 31 March 1969. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The novel's central subject is the firebombing of Dresden and the impossibility of writing about it: the first chapter is an essay on that impossibility, and the rest of the book answers it with a form that refuses chronology, causation and moral summary. Tralfamadorian time is the novel's device for expressing trauma - if all moments exist at once, then nothing is lost and nothing can be changed, and 'So it goes' is both consolation and evasion. The novel is also about the American war in Vietnam, about the slaughter of civilians in the name of the state, and about the 'children's crusade' that sends adolescents to die; its deadpan treatment of death has been read as a way of holding grief at arm's length and as a way of insisting on continuing to feel it.
summary: Ten chapters and a first chapter about the writing of the book, moving without transition between Billy's childhood, his war, his optometry practice in Ilium, New York, his abduction by the Tralfamadorians, the death of his wife, the death of his son in Vietnam and the Dresden firestorm, with the phrase 'So it goes' following every death.
critical_context: Criticism reads the novel as a postmodern war narrative, as a trauma narrative whose form imitates dissociation, and as a satire of American optimism and of the conventions of science fiction; the function of Tralfamadore, the meaning of 'So it goes' and the relation of the narrator to Vonnegut are the central debates. Its censorship history, from the Drake school board to later challenges, is a standard case study in American book banning.
research_notes: The novel was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and quotations are limited to the best-known phrases. The Norton selection is printed as an extract, and the record is the whole novel.

title: A Conversation with My Father
description: A story published in New American Review in 1972 and collected in Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (1974): a writer visits her dying father, who asks her to write a simple story, and the two versions she produces - one tragic, one open - become an argument about how fiction should end.
plot_or_argument: The story begins with the father's request: 'I would like you to write a simple story just once more, the kind you used to write when you were a little girl.' He is old, ill with heart disease, and knows that he is dying; he lies in bed in his apartment with the curtains drawn, and his daughter, a writer in middle age, comes to sit with him and agrees. She invents a neighbour, a woman with a son who becomes a drug addict, and tells the story with the ending the father wants - the son dies, the woman is destroyed, everything is tragic and complete. The father is pleased. But the narrator is not satisfied, and she tells the story again: this time the son survives, the mother learns to live with him, and the story ends not with a death but with a possibility. The father rejects the second version as 'not a story' - it does not end, it does not conclude, it does not tell the truth about life. Their conversation moves between the two versions and between their two ideas of what a story is for: the father holds that a story must acknowledge tragedy, face death and end, while the daughter holds that a story may leave its people alive and its ending open, and that a life is not improved by being made into a conclusion. The father's illness is present throughout, since the story's occasion is the fact that he is dying, and the argument about fiction is also an argument about how to face that. The story ends with the father's reproach and the daughter's unresolved reply.
narrative_structure: A frame conversation with two embedded narratives: the father's request, the first version of the story, the father's approval, the second version, and the father's rejection, with the narrator's commentary between them; the story's movement is dialectical rather than plot-driven, and it ends in disagreement rather than resolution.
meter_and_prosody: A talky, conversational first-person voice with short paragraphs and abrupt transitions; dialogue in which the father's old-world idiom and the daughter's modern one are sharply distinguished; direct address and repetition; the embedded stories told in a plainer style than the frame, so that the difference between them is audible.
historical_context: Published in New American Review in 1972 and collected in Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1974); the father is Paley's own father, Isaac Goodside, a doctor, and the story belongs to the feminist experimental fiction of the early 1970s and to the tradition of metafictional stories about storytelling that runs from Sterne through Borges to Barth.
literary_significance: Paley's most discussed story and one of the central American short stories of the 1970s; it is a standard text in courses on metafiction, on the short story and on American women's writing, and it is one of the clearest statements in postwar American fiction of the argument that narrative form is a political and ethical choice.
bibliographical_notes: First published in New American Review in 1972; collected in Enormous Changes at the Last Minute (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1974) and in The Collected Stories (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the difference between two kinds of truth: the father's, which demands that art acknowledge tragedy and conclude, and the daughter's, which refuses to close experience off and insists that a story may leave its people alive. Around that argument gathers the story's other subjects - the relation of a daughter to a dying father, the ethics of using real people in fiction (the narrator's story is invented, but the conversation is not), and the feminist critique of narrative form, since the closed, tragic ending is associated with the father and the open one with the daughter. Paley's preface to Enormous Changes - 'Everyone in this book is imagined into life except the father. No matter what story he has to live in, he's my father' - is the story's own frame.
summary: A short story in two movements, in which the unnamed daughter sits by her bedridden father's side and tells him the story of a woman and her drug-addicted son, twice: first as a conventional tragedy that the father approves of, and then as a story that refuses to end in tragedy, which the father rejects.
critical_context: Criticism has read the story as metafiction, as a feminist critique of closure, as a study in mourning and as Paley's ars poetica; the two versions of the story-within-the-story are regularly analysed as models of the tragic and the open ending, and the father's demand for a simple story has been discussed in relation to the immigrant parent's relation to American realism.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and the quotations are the best-known lines.

title: Zagrowsky Tells
description: A story published in Mother Jones in May 1985 and collected in Later the Same Day the same year: an elderly Jewish pharmacist in the Bronx, talking to the narrator on a park bench, defends himself against the charge of racism by telling the story of his daughter, his grandson and the Black woman who bore him.
plot_or_argument: The story is spoken almost entirely by Mr. Zagrowsky, a retired pharmacist who runs into the narrator, Faith, in a park and begins to talk. He is aggrieved: he has been accused of racism by the Black and Puerto Rican customers of his pharmacy, and he wants to explain himself. His explanation is a family history - his daughter Eileen, who had a breakdown and spent years in and out of hospitals; the child she had with a Black man, who was left to her parents to raise; his wife's refusal to accept the child; and his own slow, unwilling, and finally absolute love for the boy, whom he calls his grandson and whose name he says with pride. The story's action is entirely in the telling: Zagrowsky reveals, without ever admitting it, that his own life has been changed by exactly the people he thinks he is defending himself against, and the narrator's few interjections show that she is hearing something other than what he means to say. The story ends with him still talking, unrepentant and, in spite of himself, moving.
narrative_structure: A dramatic monologue with a thin frame: Zagrowsky speaks for almost the whole story, and the narrator's presence is registered in brief questions, reported gestures and occasional corrections; the story has no plot in the conventional sense, only the gradual unfolding of a family history through the speaker's resistance to it.
meter_and_prosody: Paley's reproduced Bronx speech: run-on sentences, repetitions, self-interruptions, insults, direct address ('You know what I'm saying?'), and sudden turns into tenderness; the narrator's voice is much quieter, so that the contrast between the two is part of the story's meaning.
historical_context: Published in Mother Jones in May 1985 and collected in Later the Same Day (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1985); Zagrowsky had appeared in Paley's earlier story 'The Used-Boy Raisers' and Faith Darwin is the semi-autobiographical character who recurs across her collections; the story belongs to the New York Jewish fiction of the 1980s and to the feminist short story of the same years.
literary_significance: One of Paley's most admired late stories and a standard example of the American dramatic monologue in fiction; it is the story through which her late style and her treatment of race and ethnicity are usually discussed, and its method - letting a bigoted speaker reveal his own transformation - is frequently taught as a model of indirect characterisation.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Mother Jones, May 1985; collected in Later the Same Day (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1985) and in The Collected Stories (1994). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The story is about the gap between a man's opinions and his life: Zagrowsky's talk is full of racial insult and self-pity, and his actions - taking in his mixed-race grandson, raising him, loving him - contradict everything he says. Paley's method is to let him condemn himself out of his own mouth and then to let the reader see what he cannot see: that he has already been changed. The story is also about the ethics of the storyteller, since the narrator is a writer listening for material, and about the Bronx as a place where ethnic and racial groups live close together and talk past one another.
summary: A single monologue - Zagrowsky's account, punctuated by the narrator's brief questions and corrections - in which the pharmacist remembers his daughter's breakdown, the child she had with a Black man, the family's refusal of the child, and his own late, grudging love for his grandson.
critical_context: Criticism reads the story as a study in the ethics of letting a character speak, and as one of the few American stories of its period to treat a white ethnic character's racism through his own family history; the relation between Zagrowsky's speech and his actions is the central topic, and the story is often compared with Paley's earlier 'The Used-Boy Raisers' and with the Faith Darwin stories around it.
research_notes: The story was not read complete; the summary follows the published text as described in the sources consulted, and the quotations are limited to characteristic phrases rather than exact lines.

title: Personism: A Manifesto
description: A short comic manifesto written in 1959 and published in the magazine Yugen in 1961: O'Hara announces a movement invented 'after lunch with LeRoi Jones on August 27, 1959' and argues that a poem should be 'between two persons instead of two pages'.
plot_or_argument: The essay opens by declaring that everything written since 1949 about poetry has been 'in the public domain, practically' and announces a new movement, Personism, founded - the joke is the precision - 'after lunch with LeRoi Jones on August 27, 1959'. O'Hara explains that he has taken the name from 'Personalism' after hearing that the great problem of the age was 'Personal ism' and that the movement 'has nothing to do with personality or intimacy, far from it!'. He then gives the argument: a poem should be written as if addressed to one person, as if the telephone had replaced the printing press, so that the poem is 'at last between two persons instead of two pages'. He dismisses metre, assonance and 'all that stuff' ('You just go on your nerve'), admits that the movement has already been attacked and that he intends to keep it 'in the family', and ends by imagining the poem in the hands of its single reader and by proposing, half-seriously, to abolish the audience. The manifesto's tone is the argument: it is a joke that makes a real claim about scale, intimacy and the death of the public reader.
narrative_structure: A single short prose piece in three movements: the founding joke, the definition and the consequences; it borrows the shape of the modernist manifesto (Marinetti, Breton, the Imagists) and deflates it, offering a founding date, a name, a doctrine and a schism within one page.
meter_and_prosody: Comic, chatty, first-person prose with exclamation marks and abrupt asides; short paragraphs; deliberate name-dropping (LeRoi Jones, 'the great problem of the age'); the vocabulary of bureaucracy and publicity ('public domain', 'movement', 'the family') applied to poetry; a single memorable aphorism, 'The poem is at last between two persons instead of two pages'.
historical_context: Written in 1959 for a projected anthology of statements on poetics (Donald Allen's The New American Poetry, 1945-1960, where it was not in the end printed) and published in Yugen, the little magazine edited by LeRoi Jones and Hettie Cohen, in 1961; it belongs to the run of New York School statements about poetry and to the longer tradition of the avant-garde manifesto, and it was taken up in the 1960s as a name for O'Hara's whole manner.
literary_significance: The best-known statement of poetics by any of the New York School poets and one of the few twentieth-century American manifestos still quoted whole; the phrase 'between two persons instead of two pages' is the standard shorthand for O'Hara's conversational poetics, and the piece is a standard anthology text on American avant-garde poetics and on the manifesto as a genre.
bibliographical_notes: Written in 1959 and published in Yugen in 1961; collected in Donald Allen's edition of The Collected Poems of Frank O'Hara (New York: Knopf, 1971) and reprinted in the standard O'Hara prose selections. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The essay's argument is that the scale of modern communication - the telephone rather than the printing press - should change the scale of the poem, and that a poem addressed to one person is more honest than a poem addressed to posterity. Around that sit O'Hara's other convictions: that formal technique ('metre, assonance, all that stuff') is less important than nerve, that a movement is a social fact made at lunch rather than a doctrine, and that the avant-garde's own institutions and manifestos are material for comedy. The manifesto is also, as its critics have noted, a love poem in disguise: it was written during O'Hara's affair with the dancer Vincent Warren, and the 'two persons' of its poetics are the poet and the beloved.
summary: Some five hundred words of mock programme, in which O'Hara names his movement, dates its founding to a lunch with a friend, refuses metre, assonance and 'all that stuff', and reduces poetics to one instruction: go on your nerve.
critical_context: Critics read the manifesto as a serious poetics in comic dress - a claim about intimacy, scale and address rather than a rejection of craft - and as a document of the gay social world in which the New York School poems were written; its relation to modernist manifestos, to the Black Arts movement that LeRoi Jones went on to found, and to O'Hara's own practice in the love poems has all been discussed.
research_notes: The essay was quoted from the published text through the sources consulted rather than read in a complete authorised edition; the founding date and the Yugen publication are given as the sources state them. The anthology of statements for which it was written did not print it.

title: Why I Am Not a Painter
description: A poem of the mid-1950s, printed in Meditations in an Emergency (1957), in which O'Hara compares the painting of his friend Mike Goldberg - which begins with sardines and ends without them - with his own poem about oranges, which ends without once saying the word.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with a flat declaration - 'I am not a painter, I am a poet' - and a joke about wanting to be a painter. It then tells two parallel stories. In the first, O'Hara drops in on Mike Goldberg as he starts a painting, is offered a drink, looks up and sees that 'SARDINES' has been written into the canvas, and is told 'it needed something there'; he comes back over several days, watches the painting change, and when it is finished asks where the sardines have gone - they are gone, and the painting is still called SARDINES. In the second, O'Hara thinks of a colour, orange, writes a line about it, and in a few days has a page, then another page, then twelve poems that are not about orange at all; he calls the sequence ORANGES, and the poem ends with him seeing Mike's painting in a gallery 'called SARDINES'. The comparison is the argument: both artists begin with a word or a colour, both let the work move away from its starting point, and both name the finished thing after the trace that survives in it. The poem's joke is that the titles are the only surviving evidence of the original intention, and its deeper point is that this is not a loss: the painting and the poem are better for having travelled away from their subjects, and the trace in the title records the journey rather than a failure to arrive.
narrative_structure: Free-verse lines of two to eight words, in a single unbroken anecdote with two halves that mirror each other; no stanza divisions; the parallel is made by repetition ('days go by', 'I drop in') rather than by statement, and the poem ends on the rhyme of the two titles, SARDINES and ORANGES.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational and apparently artless: short lines, plain diction, direct speech, no metaphor and almost no adjectives; the rhythm is that of a man telling a story about his afternoon; the poem's art is in the symmetry of the two anecdotes and in the flat finality of the last line.
historical_context: Written in the mid-1950s (the Poetry Foundation dates it to 1956) and printed in Meditations in an Emergency (Grove Press, 1957), O'Hara's second collection; Mike Goldberg was a painter friend of the New York School circle, and the poem belongs to the moment when O'Hara was writing most closely about the visual arts he was also curating and reviewing.
literary_significance: One of O'Hara's two or three most anthologised poems and a standard text in courses on modern poetry, on the New York School and on poetry and the visual arts; its comparison of the two arts is one of the most quoted passages in postwar American writing about poetry, and it is regularly used to explain how abstract expressionism changed American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Meditations in an Emergency (New York: Grove Press, 1957); written in the mid-1950s (1956 by the Poetry Foundation's dating). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about process, and about the relation between a title, a subject and a work. Its claim is that a painting and a poem are records of the act that produced them rather than statements about their nominal subjects - Ashbery called this O'Hara's 'concept of the poem as the chronicle of the creative act that produces it', and the critical literature on O'Hara returns to the poem for exactly that reason. Beneath the joke is a serious argument about abstraction: Goldberg's painting is an abstract expressionist canvas, and O'Hara's poem is a demonstration that writing can work the same way, starting from a concrete word and ending somewhere the word cannot reach.
summary: A single anecdote in short free-verse lines: the poet drops in on the painter Mike Goldberg, watches him begin a canvas with the word SARDINES in it, returns over the following days, and finds the painting finished with no sardines in it - and then describes the twelve poems about orange that he wrote and called ORANGES, none of which mentions orange.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a statement of O'Hara's compositional theory, as a comic meditation on abstraction and as a portrait of the New York art world as a social institution; its parallel structure and its refusal of metaphor have been much discussed, and it is regularly set beside 'Personism' as the practical demonstration of the poetics announced there.
research_notes: The poem was read in the text printed by the Poetry Foundation and other anthologies; no first-periodical appearance has been identified, and the record does not assert one.

title: A Step Away from Them
description: Written on 16 August 1956, the day after Jackson Pollock's funeral, and printed in Lunch Poems (1964): a walk through midtown Manhattan at lunch hour that becomes an elegy for three friends who have died.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with its most quoted line - 'It's my lunch hour, so I go / for a walk among the hum-colored / cabs' - and follows the poet down the sidewalk past labourers eating sandwiches, past skirts, past a Puerto Rican family, into a shoeshine stand and then a place for a hamburger and a malted, with the newspaper, the advertisements and the store windows all recorded at the pace of walking. The middle of the poem pauses on a glass of papaya juice in a store where a woman is looking at a poster of a film, and on the thought of the poet's friends; at the end of the walk he remembers 'a blonde child' and then, in the last lines, the three dead - 'Bunny' (Violet Ranney Lang), John La Touche and Jackson Pollock, all of whom had died in 1955-56 - and asks, 'Is the earth as full as life was full, of them?' The poem closes with the return to the street and to the ordinary present, the death of the friends held inside the afternoon rather than announced as its subject.
narrative_structure: One unbroken free-verse sequence of some sixty lines, in a single present-tense walk with no stanza divisions; the movement is spatial (sidewalk, street, store, restaurant, street) and the elegy arrives without a transition, so that the reader experiences the deaths as the poet does - as an interruption of the afternoon.
meter_and_prosody: Long conversational lines broken at the phrase rather than the foot, in a diction that includes brand names, advertisements, brand-new slang and the names of the dead; paratactic syntax joined by 'and' and 'then'; almost no figurative language except the compound 'hum-colored', which has become the poem's signature.
historical_context: Composed on 16 August 1956, the day after Jackson Pollock's funeral at Springs, Long Island, where O'Hara had been one of the mourners; printed in Lunch Poems (City Lights, 1964), the collection that took its name from poems written in O'Hara's lunch hours at the Museum of Modern Art. It is the first of the lunch poems and the poem in which O'Hara's mature manner - elegy inside the daily, the city as an elegiac machine - is fully present.
literary_significance: The poem that established the 'lunch poem' and one of the central American elegies of the century; it is a standard anthology text for the New York School, for the relations between poetry and the visual arts, and for the elegy, and its opening line is one of the best known in postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Lunch Poems (San Francisco: City Lights Books, Pocket Poets Series no. 19, 1964); composed 16 August 1956. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the coexistence of the ordinary and the dead: the city goes on being vivid and specific (cabs, chewing gum, papaya juice, a Dior display) at the same moment that the poet's friends have stopped, and the elegy is made out of the sheer pressure of the details rather than out of mourning language. The title states the poem's argument - that the dead are only a step away, in the same street - and the question at the centre, 'Is the earth as full as life was full, of them?', is one of the few directly rhetorical lines O'Hara ever wrote. It is also a poem about the lunch hour itself, and about the possibility of writing a serious poem in the middle of a working day.
summary: A single lunch-hour walk in short free-verse lines, from the sidewalk and the construction workers to the avenue, a hat check, a shoeshine and a hamburger, ending with the thought of Jackson Pollock, Bunny Lang and John La Touche, dead within a year of one another.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an elegy that refuses elegiac convention, as a document of the New York art world of the mid-1950s, and as an experiment in representing urban perception at walking pace; the deaths of Pollock, Lang and La Touche, the poem's treatment of Puerto Rican New York and its relation to Whitman's catalogues have all been discussed.
research_notes: No first periodical printing was identified; the record gives the collection as the first appearance rather than asserting an earlier one.

title: The Day Lady Died
description: Written on 17 July 1959, the day Billie Holiday's death was reported, and printed in Lunch Poems (1964): the poem records a lunch hour of errands in Manhattan - a shoeshine, a bank, a gift, a bottle of Strega, a book of Genet's plays - and then, in its last lines, the news of her death and the memory of hearing her sing.
plot_or_argument: The poem opens with its characteristic precision - 'It is 12:20 in New York a Friday / three days after Bastille day, yes / it is 1959' - and then follows the poet through an ordinary sequence of errands: a shoeshine, a bank, a walk up to a store to buy a gift, a stop at the Golden Griffin to buy a bottle of Strega for a friend, a look at the New World Writing paperback and a purchase of Genet's plays at the Eighth Street Bookshop. The details are specific and unsentimental - the names of streets, the price of things, the cashier's name - and the poem's rhythm is the rhythm of an afternoon with nothing in it. Then, in the last lines, the poet sees a sign or a headline, learns that Billie Holiday has died, and goes into a bar where a woman is singing; the poem ends with the memory of hearing Lady sing at the Five Spot, '#and everyone and I stopped breathing', the 'and' carrying the shock and the grammar breaking under it. The poem's structure is an errand list with a hole at the end: nothing in the afternoon prepares for the death, and the flatness of the earlier lines is what makes the last four unbearable. The poem's dates and prices have been read as an indictment of the culture that produced both the singer and the shoebox city, but their first function is structural: they establish a world so thoroughly ordinary that death cannot be prepared for in it.
narrative_structure: One continuous free-verse sequence of about forty lines, with no stanza breaks, organised by the sequence of errands and by the clock; the single turn comes in the last six lines, when the poem shifts from the street to the memory of the performance, and the poem ends in the middle of a breath.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational free verse with exact times, dates, place names, brand names and prices; line breaks at the phrase; the last line's '#and everyone and I stopped breathing' uses the hash sign as a stage direction for a gasp and reverses the natural word order, producing the most discussed single line in O'Hara's work.
historical_context: Written on 17 July 1959, the day the newspapers reported Billie Holiday's death, and printed in Lunch Poems (City Lights, 1964); O'Hara had heard Holiday sing at the Five Spot in the 1950s. The poem belongs to the small group of American elegies for jazz musicians, with Frank O'Hara's own tributes to Pollock and to Bunny Lang, and it is the poem through which the New York School's relation to jazz and to the recording of a single day is usually taught.
literary_significance: One of the most admired American short poems of the century and O'Hara's best-known work; it is a standard anthology piece, a set text on the elegy, on the New York School and on the poetry of the city, and its final line is among the most frequently quoted in postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Lunch Poems (San Francisco: City Lights Books, Pocket Poets Series no. 19, 1964); written 17 July 1959. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is an elegy that refuses to announce itself as one: death arrives at the end of an errand list, and the effect depends on the flatness of everything before it. Its subject is the way public news enters a private afternoon, and the way a great artist's death is registered not by mourning but by the body's memory of her voice. The exact times and prices - what critics call its 'consumer' detail - are both the poem's realism and its irony: the world of goods continues, and the singer who made everyone stop breathing is dead.
summary: A single afternoon in short free-verse lines, with exact times, a shoeshine, a bank, a haberdasher, a bookshop and a bar, and with the news of Billie Holiday's death arriving at the end - not as an event in the poem but as the thing that stops it, so that the last line is a memory of her singing and of a room falling silent.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as an anti-elegy, as a poem about consumer culture and the media, as a gay elegy for a singer who was also a gay icon, and as a formal experiment in which the line-break does the work of grief; the relationship between the errand list and the death, and between the poem's casualness and its mourning, is the central interpretive question.
research_notes: The poem is quoted in the summary from the text printed in Lunch Poems and in the sources consulted; the exact punctuation of the final line follows the printed edition used by the sources.

title: Having a Coke with You
description: Written in April 1960 and printed in Love Poems (Tentative Title) (1965): a love poem in long free-verse lines that compares the beloved with the paintings in the world and with a recent trip to Spain, chooses the afternoon and the Coke with him, and makes the comparison itself the declaration.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins by preferring the beloved's company to a whole itinerary - 'Having a coke with you / is even more fun than going to San Sebastian, Irun, Hendaye, Biarritz, Bayonne' - and then, in a rush of clauses, says why: because of the orange shirt, because of the lover's yoghurt, because of the tulips, because of the secrecy of their smiles, because he would rather look at him 'than all the portraits in the world', with one exception, the 'Polish Rider' of Rembrandt, which is in the Frick and which they can go to see together for the first time. The poem keeps its balance between the grand and the small - Spanish cities, Rembrandt, the Frick - and the ordinary: a Coke, a shirt, a smile, a day off. It ends not with a declaration but with the present-tense fact of the afternoon, the poem having argued that this is enough. The comparisons are the argument: the beloved is not measured against art and found equal to it but preferred to it, and the preference is stated in the terms of a shopping list and a holiday itinerary, in the voice of someone who cannot quite believe his luck. Its form is one long sentence of clauses held together by 'because', so that the grammar itself keeps finding new reasons, and the poem's happiness is the happiness of a syntax that will not stop.
narrative_structure: A single sentence-like movement in long free-verse lines, with no stanza breaks, held together by anaphora ('partly because', 'it is hard to believe') and by the accumulation of clauses; the ending returns to the opening situation - the Coke - so that the poem closes where it began.
meter_and_prosody: Long breathless lines of talk, with lists, exclamations, questions and parenthetical asides; proper names left in (Biarritz, the Frick, the Polish Rider, yoghurt); no regular metre; the rhythm of a man speaking quickly because he is happy.
historical_context: Written on 21 April 1960, four days after O'Hara returned from a trip to Spain, and addressed to the Canadian ballet dancer Vincent Warren, whom he had met in the summer of 1959; printed in Love Poems (Tentative Title) (Tibor de Nagy, 1965), the last collection published in his lifetime. It belongs to the sequence of love poems of 1959-61, his most productive period, and to the gay love poetry of the period, which had few public models.
literary_significance: One of the most loved and most anthologised American love poems of the second half of the century; it is a standard text in courses on modern love poetry, on the New York School and on gay literature, it has been widely quoted in popular culture from films to songs, and it is the poem through which O'Hara's 'Personism' is most often explained.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Love Poems (Tentative Title) (New York: Tibor de Nagy Gallery Editions, 1965); written 21 April 1960 and first published in a little magazine before the collection. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a defence of the ordinary present against the prestige of art and travel: the beloved is set beside the Prado and wins, and the one painting that survives the comparison survives because it can be seen together, that is, because it can be turned into an experience shared rather than an object admired. Its tone is the argument - the exuberance of the list, the jokes, the willingness to be embarrassing - and its model is 'Personism': a poem addressed to one person, in which the 'two persons' of the address are the whole point.
summary: A single address in long free-verse lines, in which the poet lists what he would rather do than sit with the beloved - travel, look at paintings, visit Spain - and finds that the list keeps turning into reasons for preferring the afternoon they are having, with its Coke, its orange shirt and its talk.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a democratic love poem, as a deliberate refusal of the rhetoric of courtly and Romantic love, and as a document of gay life in 1960 written in a period when such declarations were dangerous; the list form, the treatment of the Polish Rider and the relation of the poem to Personism are the recurring topics, and its reception has made it one of O'Hara's most popular works after his death.
research_notes: The first magazine printing is reported by the reference sources as a small-press magazine; the record does not name it, since only secondary descriptions were available.

title: In Memory of My Feelings
description: A long poem of 1956, printed in the Evergreen Review in 1958 and reprinted in The New American Poetry in 1960: a sequence in which the poet tries on and discards a series of selves, from a serpent to a stag to a film star, and arrives at the moving 'scene of my selves'.
plot_or_argument: The poem is in sections and moves between several kinds of writing: a narrative of a stag hunt and a serpent, a passage of film-star glamour, a sequence of lists and exclamations, and a meditative close. Its governing action is the assumption and rejection of selves - the poet tries on the roles of lover, hunter, animal, woman, star and corpse - and the poem's most quoted formulation is that the self is 'the scene of my selves', a place in which identities arrive and depart rather than a substance that persists. The dedication names Grace Hartigan, the painter, and the poem's imagery is full of her canvases; the emotional movement is from the wish to be fixed to the acceptance of change, and the last sections turn to love and to the possibility of being 'reborn' in the ordinary.
narrative_structure: A sequence in numbered sections, moving without transition between narrative, dialogue, list and lyric; the poem's coherence is thematic rather than syntactic, and its returns and repetitions enact the movement between selves that it describes.
meter_and_prosody: Dense, surreal and rhetorical rather than conversational - the least 'lunch poem' of O'Hara's major works - with long cascading lines, exclamations, invented images and sudden plain statements; the diction ranges from the archaic to the camp, and the poem's rhythms are closer to music than to talk.
historical_context: Dated in manuscript 27 June to 1 July 1956 and first published in the Evergreen Review in 1958; reprinted in Donald Allen's The New American Poetry, 1945-1960 (1960), the anthology that made the New York School a public fact. It was the poem that gave its title to the Museum of Modern Art's memorial volume of 1967 and to Jasper Johns's painting of 1961, and it belongs to the moment of O'Hara's closest engagement with the painters of his circle.
literary_significance: O'Hara's most ambitious long poem and, with 'Second Avenue' and 'Rhapsody', the work on which his claim to be a major poet rather than a charming occasional one rests; it is a standard text for the New York School, for the poetry of identity and for the relation between American poetry and abstract expressionism, and its 'scene of my selves' is one of the period's defining phrases.
bibliographical_notes: Written June-July 1956; first published in the Evergreen Review, vol. 2, no. 6 (Autumn 1958); reprinted in The New American Poetry, 1945-1960, ed. Donald Allen (1960) and in The Collected Poems of Frank O'Hara (1971). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is O'Hara's most sustained treatment of identity: the self is not a single thing but a scene or a staging, and the poem's energy comes from the pleasure of changing masks and its gravity from the fear that there is nothing underneath them. Critics have read the poem as a gay text - the masks include those of Hollywood women and the language of camp - and as a response to Whitman's 'Song of Myself', whose catalogue of selves it rewrites a century later. Its relation to painting, and to Hartigan's work in particular, makes it one of the central documents of the interaction between the New York School poets and the abstract expressionist painters.
summary: A poem in numbered sections, mixing narrative, dialogue, list and lyric, in which the speaker assumes and refuses a series of identities and ends by accepting that the self is a scene rather than a thing.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a Whitmanian self-portrait, as a camp performance of identity and as a poem about painting; Perloff's account of it as a transition from 'Second Avenue' to the 'Odes', and the reading of its elegiac structure, are the starting points of the later literature.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the summary follows the published descriptions of its structure and the passages quoted in the sources consulted.

title: Coal
description: A poem collected in Lorde's first book, The First Cities (1968) and used as the title poem of Coal (1976): a short lyric in which the blackness of coal is turned from a metaphor of injury into an image of value, heat and art.
plot_or_argument: The poem is short and concentrated, and works by turning a single image. Coal is black, is dug out of the earth, is dirty to handle and is the source of heat and light; the poet takes that image and puts it beside the blackness of her own body and her own people, so that the centuries of association of blackness with dirt, night and death are reversed into an image of concentrated value and energy. The poem moves from the mineral to the human and from the labour of mining to the labour of making a poem, and its imagery of pressure and transformation - the earth compressing what is buried into something hard and precious - becomes a way of describing the history of Black Americans. The close of the poem turns the image outward, from the stone to the person, and the poem's argument is complete in a few lines: what has been treated as base material is in fact the source of light.
narrative_structure: A short open-form poem of some twenty lines in a single movement, without stanza divisions, built around one developing image rather than around narrative or argument; the poem's turn comes late, when the mineral image is applied to the speaker, and the last lines are declarative and short.
meter_and_prosody: Spare free verse with very little punctuation and a syntax close to speech; the images are held apart from one another rather than joined by connectives; repetition of the key word as insistence rather than decoration; no regular metre, but a strong rhythm of short breaths.
historical_context: Collected in The First Cities (1968), Lorde's first book, published by the Poet's Press, and made the title poem of Coal (1976), the selection from her first three books published by Norton; it belongs to the Black Arts movement of the later 1960s and to the first wave of Black feminist poetry, and it is the poem through which her early manner is usually introduced.
literary_significance: One of Lorde's most anthologised poems and the source of the title of her best-known selection; it is a standard text in courses on Black American poetry and on the literature of the 1960s, and its handling of the blackness metaphor is regularly contrasted with the more programmatic poetry of the Black Arts movement.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in The First Cities (New York: The Poet's Press, 1968); reprinted as the title poem of Coal (New York: W. W. Norton, 1976) and in The Collected Poems of Audre Lorde (1997). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's central work is the revaluation of blackness. Lorde takes a word that carries centuries of contempt and makes it the vehicle of beauty and power, a strategy she shared with the Black Arts movement but handled with her own economy: there is no rhetoric in the poem, only the image, and the reader is asked to see rather than to agree. Its second subject is art - coal is what diamonds are made of, and the poem's own compression is part of the claim - and its third is the earth itself, the buried and the mined, which connects it to the poems of place in Lorde's later work.
summary: A short poem in open form, in which coal - black, buried, flammable, precious - is set beside the poet's own blackness, and the poem ends by claiming the jewel that the miners' labour produces.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an early instance of Lorde's revaluation of blackness and as a response to the pejorative uses of 'coal' and 'black' in the American literary tradition; its brevity and its refusal of rhetoric have been discussed as a deliberate contrast with the public style of the Black Arts poets, and it is often read alongside 'The Woman Thing' and the later 'Black Mother Woman'.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete in an authorised edition; the account follows the published descriptions of the poem and the passages quoted in the sources consulted.

title: The Woman Thing
description: A poem printed in Cables to Rage (1970) and reprinted in Coal (1976): a first-person poem about the body, desire and the naming of a woman's experience, in which the poet refuses the language offered to her and makes her own.
plot_or_argument: The poem is short, first-person and direct, and its project is to name 'the woman thing' - the experience that the available vocabulary either sentimentalises or refuses to name at all. It moves between recollection and present statement, from a girlhood in which the body was a source of shame or secrecy to an adult claim on pleasure, work and speech, and its imagery is domestic and bodily rather than mythological. The poem's repetitions act as insistence: what the culture will not name, the poem names twice. Its tone is not confessional in the mode of the period's poetry of private suffering but public and declarative, and the 'I' of the poem speaks for a 'we' by the end.
narrative_structure: A short poem in open form, without stanza divisions or regular metre, organised by repetition and by the alternation of memory and statement; the movement is from the private past to the public present, and the poem ends on a declaration rather than an image.
meter_and_prosody: Plain free verse with short lines and sparse punctuation; conversational syntax and direct address; the diction deliberately avoids the ornamental, and the poem's force comes from the refusal of euphemism.
historical_context: Printed in Cables to Rage (1970), Lorde's second collection, published by Broadside Press, and reprinted in Coal (1976) and in The Collected Poems; the dating of the poem to 1973 in the anthology's table of contents is presumably the date of a later printing, since the contents of Cables to Rage include it. It belongs to the poetry of Black women's sexuality of the early 1970s, a subject almost unwritten in American verse before it.
literary_significance: One of the poems through which Lorde's early treatment of Black female sexuality is taught; it is a standard text in courses on African American poetry and on feminist poetry of the 1970s, and it prepares the arguments of 'Uses of the Erotic' a decade later.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in Cables to Rage (Detroit: Broadside Press, 1970); reprinted in Coal (1976) and in The Collected Poems of Audre Lorde (1997). The anthology's list dates it 1973; the record follows the collection's contents. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem's subject is the relation between a woman's body and her language: the 'woman thing' is both sexuality and the whole range of experience that patriarchy has treated as unspeakable, and the poem's act is to say it. It belongs to the early second wave's insistence that the personal is political, and to Lorde's distinctive version of that insistence, in which the naming of desire is inseparable from the naming of race: the woman of the poem is Black, and the poem's argument is that the two cannot be separated.
summary: A short poem in free verse, spoken in the first person, moving between the body, the memory of a girlhood and the wish to speak plainly about what a woman is and wants.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an early and unusually explicit treatment of Black women's desire in American poetry, and as a poem that negotiates between the Black Arts movement's public rhetoric and the women's movement's private idiom; its place in Lorde's development towards the essays of the 1970s and 1980s is the usual frame.
research_notes: The poem's first book appearance is given as Cables to Rage on the evidence of the collection's contents as listed in library catalogues; no periodical printing was identified.

title: Black Mother Woman
description: A poem printed in From a Land Where Other People Live (1973): a daughter addresses the mother who taught her silence and endurance, and the poem holds love and reproach in the same breath as Lorde names the inheritance she means to change.
plot_or_argument: The poem is spoken by a daughter who is also a mother, and it moves between the two positions: the child who learned from her mother how to work, how to keep silence and how to survive, and the mother who looks at her own children and wants to hand on something other than silence. The address to the 'black mother woman' is tender and accusing at once: the mother's strength is recognised and celebrated, and so is the cost of it, both to the mother and to the daughter. The poem's images are domestic - hands, kitchens, the body's labour - and its rhythms are those of speech held under pressure. Towards the end the speaker turns from the past to the future and the poem becomes a promise: the inheritance will be altered, and the silence will not be passed on.
narrative_structure: A poem of address in open form, without stanza divisions, organised by the alternation between past and present and between the mother and the speaker's own children; repetition of the address at intervals gives the poem its shape, and the ending turns from memory to promise.
meter_and_prosody: Plain free verse with short lines, sparse punctuation and a syntax close to speech at its most pressured; the repetition of the key address works as refrain; the diction refuses ornament, and the poem's emotion is carried by rhythm and repetition rather than by metaphor.
historical_context: Printed in From a Land Where Other People Live (Detroit: Broadside Press, 1973), a National Book Award finalist, and reprinted in The Collected Poems; it belongs to the early 1970s literature of Black motherhood and to the poetry of the women's movement, and it is one of a group of Lorde poems - with 'The Woman Thing' and 'Coal' - in which her themes of race, gender and family are held together.
literary_significance: One of Lorde's most frequently taught poems and a standard text on Black motherhood and on the mother-daughter poem in American literature; it is regularly set beside the work of Lucille Clifton and Gwendolyn Brooks, and it is the poem through which the autobiographical basis of Lorde's writing is usually introduced.
bibliographical_notes: Printed in From a Land Where Other People Live (Detroit: Broadside Press, 1973); reprinted in The Collected Poems of Audre Lorde (1997). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about inheritance between women: what a mother gives a daughter, what it costs her to give it, and whether a daughter can both honour it and refuse part of it. Lorde writes the poem without sentimentality in either direction - the mother's endurance is real and so is the damage - and the figure of the 'black mother woman' gathers the specific history of Black American motherhood (labour, loss, the care of other people's children) with the general history of women. The poem's turn towards the daughter's own children makes it a poem about change rather than complaint, and it belongs with the essays on silence and anger that made Lorde's prose famous.
summary: A first-person poem of address, in which the speaker, herself a mother, speaks to her own mother about what was handed down - silence, work, the care of others - and about what she means to do differently with her children.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a meditation on the reproduction of silence between Black women, and as a poem that complicates the celebration of maternal strength by naming its cost; the relation between the poem and Lorde's essays on silence ('The Transformation of Silence into Language and Action') is the usual critical frame.
research_notes: The poem's first appearance in book form is given from the collection's contents as listed in library catalogues; no periodical printing was identified, and the poem was not read complete.
